title: Korea's Top Bank CEOs Face Parliament Over Missed AI Attack Warning
summary:
Documents from the Financial Security Institute reveal South Korea warned financial firms of AI agent attacks on Sept. 17, about two weeks before the ARTEX tool was used to breach multiple institutions. This briefing, attended by about 160 security officials, disclosed the country's first confirmed AI agent intrusion involving a DeepSeek-based tool used to exploit Oracle WebLogic systems. The CEOs of South Korea's five largest banks are now due before parliament on Oct. 19 to answer for security failures that left banks vulnerable to these campaigns.

The intrusions targeted at least nine banks, including Shinhan, KB Kookmin, and Hana Bank, exposing data of 68,000 customers. CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a 26 year old financially motivated operator in China who combined ARTEX with Claude Code and Grok 4.6. The attacker was identified after leaving his own server open, exposing session logs and an AI-generated resume containing his personal identity and location in Guangdong. The developer of ARTEX subsequently took the tool closed source after the breaches.

selectedTweets.text:
This hacker is truly legendary. A complete amateur.

1. He left directory listing enabled on his own server, so researchers could figure out who he was with barely any effort.
2. They found files like CLAUDE.md and went through his Claude Code sessions.
3. There were questions like, “Where can I sell this data?”
4. He’d also asked, “Can you write my résumé?” That pretty much handed them all his personal information.
5. Apparently, he’s a student at South China University of Technology living in Guangdong. His name, phone number, and where he lives have all been identified.

selectedTweets.bestBit: breach at least nine South Korean banks. More than 68,000 people had their personal financial data stolen
selectedTweets.text:
AI just made your bank's database cheaper to rob.

A threat actor used ARTEX, a Chinese open-source AI pen-testing tool running on DeepSeek v4.1-flash, along with Claude Code sessions on GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6, to breach at least nine South Korean banks. More than 68,000 people had their personal financial data stolen.

At Shinhan Bank alone, loan-application data for 25,000 customers was taken: names, phone numbers, annual incomes, loan limits, and for 66 of them, national ID numbers.

The attacker wasn't sophisticated. CrowdStrike found open directories the actor left exposed on their own infrastructure, stuffed with Claude Code session histories and Chinese-language pentesting instructions. They asked Claude how to find Korean Telegram groups that buy breach data, then asked it to write them a security-researcher résumé.

CrowdStrike assesses with moderate confidence the actor is a Chinese speaker and financially motivated but hasn't established who was behind it.

Nobody cracked any encryption. They just had AI try random values on a loan-status page until one opened. Tedious grunt work you hand off to a machine.

South Korea's president said it plainly: "We have now reached a point where AI can make hacking easy for even those without special skills."

These databases are honeypots. Nothing shows a KYC rule caused this specific breach, but KYC/AML policies push companies to collect and hoard exactly the kind of data that got stolen. The cost of raiding these targets is collapsing. The cost of defending them isn't.

Hold your own keys. Hand over as little of yourself as possible. End KYC/AML.
